messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 35

He is 63, a physician who has spent most of his adult life moving quickly toward other people’s pain. For decades, he has built his identity around steadiness: calm voice, clean decisions, hands that do not shake. He is married, with a long, weathered kind of partnership that has survived residency, night call, children, and aging parents. Before the event, he thinks of himself as someone hard to rattle. He has always believed that if he understands a crisis, he can manage it.

The day of the bombing begins ordinarily enough. He is attending a medical conference in a downtown hotel, the kind of professional gathering he has gone to countless times. He remembers bad coffee, a conversation in the lobby about retirement, the mild irritation of a delayed session. Then there is a concussive blast that seems, at first, not real, as if some part of the building has slammed inward. The floor trembles. Glass breaks with a sound he later says he still hears in his molars. A second later there is screaming, then dust, then the unmistakable smell of smoke and burned material.

Training takes over before conscious thought does. He drops to the floor, then moves toward the injured. In the lobby and just outside the entrance, he sees bodies in postures no living person should hold. He tears tablecloths into strips, kneels in blood, shouts for pressure, airway, tourniquets. He works beside strangers who become an instant team. He is aware, dimly, that this is terrorism—that someone intended this—but there is no room in him yet for outrage or fear, only the narrow tunnel of triage. He locks eyes with a young woman whose leg is mangled and tells her to stay with him. He presses his hands into wounds and feels the heat leaving people. At one point he looks up and sees a shoe in the street with no owner nearby. That image returns to him later more often than the injured faces.

In the days after, he is praised for what he did. Colleagues call him heroic. News coverage loops the same footage, and his wife notices him stop in the doorway when the television is on, his face going flat before he asks her to turn it off. He tells everyone he is fine, just tired. He goes back to work quickly, telling himself that routine is the antidote to chaos. In the exam room he is still competent, still courteous, but something essential has shifted. Loud noises make his body react before his mind can catch up. A dropped instrument in clinic sends a jolt through him so sharp he feels embarrassed afterward. When an ambulance siren rises outside the hospital, his chest tightens and his jaw clenches.

Sleep becomes unreliable. He wakes before dawn with his heart pounding, unsure for a moment what year it is. Sometimes he dreams in fragments—dust, screaming, the pressure of his hands on a stranger’s wound—and sometimes he does not dream at all but still wakes exhausted, as if he has been working all night. His wife tells him he thrashes and mutters. He begins staying up later to avoid bed, sitting in the den scrolling through articles he does not absorb. He drinks one more glass of wine than he used to, not enough, he tells himself, to matter.

What troubles him most is not fear but the loss of ease. He used to enjoy conferences, crowded restaurants, holiday events at the hospital. Now he studies exits without meaning to. He chooses the seat facing the door. In hotel lobbies he feels exposed and impatient, as if lingering is a mistake. He avoids the part of downtown where the attack happened, taking longer routes and pretending traffic is the reason. On the anniversary, his wife suggests they acknowledge the day somehow, but he becomes curt and says there is nothing to mark. Still, he spends the whole afternoon restless and irritable, snapping at a nurse for a minor scheduling error and then feeling ashamed.

He is also unsettled by how the event has altered his work. Certain trauma cases pull him back instantly. The smell of cautery, a patient with blast injuries from an industrial accident, even the sight of blood on tile can narrow his vision for a second. He remains effective, but now he must fight to stay in the room. He worries about what this means, worries in the private, punishing way doctors often do—that he should be stronger, that knowledge should have protected him. When younger colleagues ask him about resilience, he gives polished answers he does not fully believe.

At home, his wife experiences him as present but less reachable. He still asks about her day, still remembers birthdays and takes out the trash, but he startles when she comes up behind him, and he has become a man who says “I’m just tired” to questions that deserve more. Sometimes she finds him standing at the kitchen window late at night, staring into the dark yard as if listening for something. He cannot easily explain that he feels both older and less solid than before, that the world no longer seems governed by the ordinary rules he trusted. He continues to work, to show up, to do what is required. But the blast remains alive in him, surfacing in sound, in sleep, in the involuntary calculations he now makes everywhere he goes.
